title: {{NAME}} and the Spell That Turned the River to Silver
moral: When you listen before you act, you often find the answer was closer than you thought.

pages.content:
The River Luminos had run clear as glass for a thousand years, so when {{NAME}} arrived at Princess Calindra's kingdom and found it flowing silver and silent, every creature on its banks standing perfectly still like painted statues, the wrongness of it landed like a stone dropped in a pond. Ripples of unease spread outward in every direction.

Calindra stood at the riverbank in her emerald gown, arms crossed and chin raised in the way that meant she was frightened but refused to let it show. Behind her, a herd of Triceratops grazed nervously among the willow trees, their crested heads bobbing with agitation, their low hooting calls carrying a strange musical sadness. The silver light from the river turned everything it touched into a painting of itself.

And at the edge of the meadow, half-hidden by morning mist, stood Luminara. She was the eldest unicorn in the valley, her coat the deep blue of the sky just before full dark, her spiral horn pulsing with a faint, anxious silver light that matched the river exactly. {{NAME}} looked from the river to Luminara and back again. The two silvers were the same silver. That was not a coincidence. That was a clue.

pages.content:
{{NAME}} did not run toward the problem. {{NAME}} walked toward the unicorn.

Luminara trembled as {{NAME}} approached, her dark eyes wide and brimming, her hooves shifting on the damp grass. Up close, the silver pulse from her horn was irregular, stuttering like a candle in a draught, and the air around her smelled of tears and cold starlight. Calindra appeared at {{NAME}}'s shoulder, her voice dropping to something careful and low. 'She hasn't spoken to anyone all morning,' the princess murmured. 'She usually sings to the river at dawn. Today she couldn't.'

{{NAME}} crouched down to Luminara's eye level, which required sitting directly in the wet grass, which ruined the amber boots entirely, and looked at her properly. Not at the horn. Not at the silver river. At her. Her expression was not mischief and it was not magic gone wrong. It was grief. Plain, simple, recognisable grief, the kind that makes everything around you go quiet and strange.

'What happened?' {{NAME}} asked, in the smallest, most careful voice available. Luminara lowered her great blue head until her velvet nose touched {{NAME}}'s cheek. And she began, at last, to tell it.

pages.content:
The story came in images and feelings more than words: a foal, silver-white and brand new, born three nights ago on the far side of the meadow. A foal who had tumbled into a narrow canyon in the dark and couldn't climb out. Luminara had poured her magic into the river, trying to make a bridge of light, but it had taken too much and the whole river had turned the colour of her fear.

Calindra was already moving before {{NAME}} had finished understanding. 'The Triceratops,' she said sharply, clapping her hands twice. The herd looked up from the willows with their enormous, musical crests tilted in attention. 'Their calls travel further than anything. If we can direct them down the canyon valley, the sound will reach the foal and keep it calm.'

Luminara lifted her head. A spark of hope moved across her face like sunrise on a still lake.

{{NAME}} vaulted onto the nearest Triceratops, a huge gentle creature named Tuba, gripping the ridge of his back as he lurched into a gallop that felt like riding a very large, very enthusiastic sofa. They thundered across the meadow, Calindra running below with her crown bouncing sideways, Luminara flying alongside in a blaze of silver and midnight blue, her hooves barely grazing the grass.

pages.content:
They found the foal at the canyon's narrowest point, a tiny creature with knees folded, coat damp and shivering, eyes like polished moons. It had called itself hoarse.

Tuba bellowed first. Then the whole herd answered from the ridge above, their great crests filling the canyon with a sound so warm and resonant it seemed to press against the cold stone walls and push the fear out through the top. The foal's ears pricked forward. Its nostrils flared. It struggled upright on legs that had forgotten how to hold it.

Luminara descended the canyon wall with a grace that seemed impossible, her hooves finding ledges narrower than a hand's width, her silver horn sending a rope of light down to the foal like a lifeline. The foal grabbed it with sheer instinct, scrambling upward, and Luminara guided each trembling step with infinite patience and a steadiness that came from somewhere deeper than magic.

When they crested the rim and stood in full sunlight, Luminara pressed her horn to her foal's forehead in the gentlest of touches. The silver drained from the river in a long, exhaled rush, leaving it clear as glass, clear as it had always been, running and laughing over its stones.

pages.content:
The foal's name, Luminara showed them that evening with a flick of light and a sound like wind chimes, was Rime. Small and miraculous and entirely pleased with itself now that it had eaten twice its own body weight in sweet meadow grass.

Calindra settled cross-legged in the willow roots with her crown finally straight, watching Rime totter importantly around the meadow. 'You knew to listen first,' she said to {{NAME}}, sounding somewhat impressed and somewhat rueful, as though she was filing it away as a lesson for herself. {{NAME}} shrugged, but it was the kind of shrug that is really a smile in disguise.

Tuba and the other Triceratops had arranged themselves in a loose, contented circle around the meadow, their crested calls fading to a low, communal hum. Luminara stood with her flank warm against {{NAME}}'s side, her horn dark and resting, her breath long and easy.

The sky turned the colour of amber and old roses as {{NAME}}'s eyes grew slower and heavier. The grass was impossibly soft. Calindra was saying something about tomorrow and exploring the northern caves, and {{NAME}} was very interested in that and absolutely planning to stay awake to hear it. Close your eyes now, brave one. Rest like the river rests. And wonder, just a little, what Rime's first gallop will look like when the morning comes.
